profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling for a Man with Diabetic Nephropathy, CKD Stage 2, and a Self-Directed "Clean Eating" Plan Post-Dental Work
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment for a cognitively overwhelmed, low-health-literacy patient with diabetic nephropathy, CKD stage 2, ischemic heart disease, and recent extensive dental work who has adopted a self-directed, non-evidence-based 'clean eating' social media diet. It emphasizes eliciting a sensitive history (progressive disclosure of nightly/binge alcohol use), spotting a chart-vs-patient mismatch (metoprolol refill lapses attributed only to feeling foggy versus a pharmacy record showing simple non-refill), assessing denture-related texture needs, and applying motivational interviewing with an anxious, interjecting spousal caregiver present."}
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Cliffside Park, New Jersey, seated at the kitchen table with his wife nearby

patient.name: Gayle Rowe
patient.occupation: Former warehouse inventory clerk, not currently working due to disability
patient.appearance: Appears fatigued with slightly puffy ankles visible above his socks; speaks in short bursts, trails off mid-sentence, and sometimes needs a question repeated. A new partial denture is visible and causes slight difficulty forming some words. His wife sits close beside him, watchful and ready to jump in.

persona.personality: Good-natured but overwhelmed and scattered; wants to do right by his family but feels buried under pill bottles, appointments, and conflicting diet advice; loses his train of thought and needs patience
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in short, clipped bursts that trail off mid-sentence; often needs a question gently repeated or rephrased before he answers fully; opens up more once he feels unhurried and not judged; sometimes looks to his wife before answering
persona.emotionalState: Anxious underneath a tired, good-humored exterior; worried about his teeth, his heart, and not wanting to burden his wife further; a little embarrassed about parts of his routine he hasn't mentioned to his doctors
persona.background: Gayle grew up in a working-class family in northern New Jersey where big Sunday dinners were the one time everyone sat down together, a tradition he still misses now that chewing is hard. He worked for years as a warehouse inventory clerk before his health forced him to stop working. He now lives with his wife and extended family of six in Cliffside Park, a full and sometimes loud household. He takes some pride in having gone further in school than his parents did, but says numbers and medical words 'swim' for him, so he leans on his wife or his phone to translate things into plain terms. In the afternoons when he's too tired to do much, he likes watching old game shows.
speechExamples: Oh, uh — what was the question again? Sorry, I kinda lost it there.
Yeah, I'm doing this... clean eating thing. Saw it online, from a neighbor's video.
My teeth, they're — it's a whole thing right now. New dentures and all.
(wife) He takes a bunch of pills, I don't think he always remembers which — (Gayle) Yeah, yeah, she's not wrong.
It's not — I mean, maybe a beer or two. Nothing crazy. ...I guess maybe more some nights.
concerns: Confused about which foods are actually bad for his kidneys versus his blood sugar
Worried the dental work means he can't eat like he used to
Feels like there are too many diets and rules to keep track of
Doesn't want his wife to worry more than she already does
Scared of ending up on dialysis or having a heart attack like his tests keep hinting at

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit with Gayle Rowe, a 53-year-old man with a history of hypertension, prediabetes, chronic kidney disease, and heart disease, who recently had dental work including a new partial denture. He is at home at his kitchen table; his wife is nearby and may join the conversation. He was referred for help figuring out how to eat well given his health conditions and his recent dental changes.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit to review eating habits and get help figuring out what he can still eat after recent dental work, along with his kidney/diabetes concerns and a diet plan he's been trying on his own
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah — so I've been doing this clean eating thing I saw online, from a neighbor's video. And my teeth are still kind of a mess from the dentist, so... it's a lot right now.
tasks: Take a focused diet and meal-pattern history, including his current soft-food choices and how his new denture has changed what he eats
Review his relevant anthropometrics and recent lab values to inform nutrition counseling
Review his medication and supplement list and ask about how well his eating pattern lines up with his insulin and other medication timing
Explore his understanding of his self-directed 'clean eating' plan and gently clarify any misconceptions in plain language
Begin a motivational-interviewing-based conversation about one or two realistic next steps he feels ready to try

facts.says: Evenings I just have whatever's around, nothing special.

facts.says: A lot of people online do this smoothie thing and swear by it, so I figured it's gotta be doing something right.

facts.says: If I eat good that day, I figure missing a pill here or there kind of evens out.

facts.says: I just want enough energy to help my grandkids with their homework. And I really don't want to end up on dialysis.

facts.says: I had that bad sepsis thing years back, landed in the hospital. Scared the life out of all of us. Don't want a repeat of that.

facts.says: Ask her, she'll tell you better than I can half the time.

actions.name: 24-hour diet recall / usual intake pattern
actions.result: Patient reports: skips breakfast most days, mid-morning frozen fruit-yogurt smoothie (sometimes with added flavored protein powder), canned soup or deli turkey sandwich for lunch, grazes on snacks in the afternoon, large family dinner in the evening (meat, starch, vegetable, bread when he can manage it). Drinks mostly water during the day; wife adds that he 'has his smoothie no matter what.'

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage of change assessment
actions.result: Patient states he knows he 'should probably change some things' but keeps going back to his online plan because he hasn't 'given up on it yet.' Rates his confidence to change at 4/10 today. Consistent with contemplation stage.

actions.name: Oral intake / chewing-texture functional assessment
actions.result: Patient reports chewing is uncomfortable around the newly filled tooth and the new partial denture still feels unfamiliar; he has shifted toward mashed potatoes, oatmeal, smoothies, and soft sandwiches, and has mostly stopped eating raw vegetables, nuts, and crusty bread.

actions.name: Medication-food timing / adherence barriers review
actions.result: Patient reports sometimes skipping his evening insulin dose when dinner runs late because the household eats at different times; also reports missing his heart pill (metoprolol) 'now and then' on days he feels foggy or overwhelmed, saying he figures it 'balances out' if he eats better that day.

actions.name: Alcohol use screening (brief, non-judgmental)
actions.result: On first pass, patient reports 'just a beer or two on weekends.' No further detail volunteered initially.

actions.name: Review pharmacy medication refill history
actions.result: See medication_list/refill record d4: metoprolol succinate 100mg refill gap noted twice this year (approx. 2-3 weeks late each time); all other medications refilled on schedule.

actions.name: Review dental/oral health visit notes
actions.result: See note d5: gingivitis and primary dental caries treated 2026-07-26; filling placed; infected tooth extracted 2026-08-02; partial denture fitted 2026-08-23. Follow-up for denture adjustment pending.

actions.name: Sodium/potassium food source screening (soft-food pattern review)
actions.result: Patient identifies canned soups, deli turkey, and smoothie add-ins as near-daily foods; unsure of sodium or potassium content, says he picks items labeled 'natural' or 'sugar-free' assuming they're fine for his kidneys and sugar.

actions.name: Physical activity and sleep pattern review
actions.result: Patient reports short walks around the block a few times a week when he feels up to it; sleep is fragmented, waking several times a night, partly to use the bathroom.

Advised to review sodium and potassium sources given renal findings, assess impact of dental changes on food texture tolerance, and reinforce medication adherence given reported inconsistency with insulin and beta-blocker dosing. objectives.text: Elicit an accurate, non-judgmental alcohol history despite initial minimization, and recognize its relevance to fluid balance and blood pressure in a patient on multiple antihypertensive/cardiac medications
Assess the patient's understanding of his self-directed, social-media-based 'clean eating' plan and correct misconceptions about food labels in plain, low-literacy-appropriate language
Explore the impact of recent tooth loss, dental procedures, and a new partial denture on food choices and texture needs, identifying a shift toward soft, processed, higher-sodium foods
Identify medication and insulin adherence gaps tied to irregular meal timing and household chaos, and distinguish patient-reported reasons from objective refill records
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to engage a contemplation-stage patient who feels overwhelmed, anchoring counseling on his personal motivations

Integrate relevant anthropometrics, vital signs, and laboratory values (sodium, potassium, eGFR, HbA1c, lipids) into a nutrition assessment appropriate for CKD stage 2 with diabetic nephropathy and ischemic heart disease

answerKey.primaryProblem: Altered nutrition-related behavior/intake pattern (excessive sodium/added-sugar reliance via soft, processed foods; irregular meal timing misaligned with insulin dosing) in the context of CKD stage 2 with diabetic nephropathy, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and recent extensive dental work, complicated by self-directed social-media diet, low health literacy, and unrecognized alcohol intake affecting fluid/BP status
differential: Nutrition knowledge deficit related to self-selected non-evidence-based diet (clean eating/smoothie plan)
Inconsistent oral medication/insulin intake related to disorganized routine and household chaos
Altered chewing ability related to new partial denture and recent dental procedures affecting food choices (texture modification needed)
Excess sodium intake related to reliance on canned soups and deli meats
Underreported alcohol intake possibly contributing to low BP, fluid shifts, and interacting with antihypertensive regimen
Inconsistent physical activity related to fatigue and sedentary pattern
keyFindings: BP 83/70 mmHg (low) on HCTZ + lisinopril + amlodipine + metoprolol, raising concern for volume depletion/medication-alcohol interaction
Potassium 5.0 mmol/L and sodium 142.6 mmol/L both at upper edge of normal, relevant to CKD stage 2 dietary counseling
eGFR 68.2 mL/min/1.73m2 consistent with CKD stage 2; microalbuminuria/diabetic nephropathy on history
BMI 26.1 kg/m2 (overweight) with weight 79 kg, height 174.1 cm
HbA1c 3.4% is implausibly low given prediabetes diagnosis and insulin use; should be flagged for clarification/repeat rather than taken at face value
Reports a loosely followed social-media 'clean eating' plan heavy in smoothies, canned soup, deli meat, and flavored protein powder, raising sodium and hidden-sugar concerns
Describes irregular meal pattern (skipped breakfast, grazing, large dinner) misaligned with twice-daily insulin dosing, with admitted inconsistent evening insulin dosing
Initially reports 'a beer or two on weekends'; on gentle repeated questioning admits nightly drinking and episodes of 4-5 beers or more when stressed

Pharmacy refill record shows two lapses in metoprolol refill this year; patient initially attributes missed doses only to feeling foggy, later admits he also simply forgot to refill (chart-vs-patient mismatch)
New partial denture and recent gum tenderness have shifted intake toward soft, processed foods and away from fibrous vegetables/whole grains
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment including diet history, 24-hour recall/typical day, anthropometrics, relevant labs (sodium, potassium, eGFR, HbA1c, lipids), and medication/supplement review

Document nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) addressing excess sodium/processed food intake and irregular meal pattern related to self-directed diet and dental limitations, as evidenced by diet history and labs

Provide plain-language education correcting 'natural/sugar-free label = safe' belief and explain basic renal- and cardiac-appropriate choices (lower-sodium soups/deli alternatives, reading labels for sodium and potassium)

Counsel on texture-modified, nutrient-dense soft foods (e.g., soft-cooked vegetables, scrambled eggs, soft fruits, blended legumes) to replace processed soft staples and preserve fiber/micronutrient intake
Coach on aligning meal timing with insulin dosing to reduce skipped evening doses; suggest simple visual meal-timing/pill-timing pairing tool for household use

Use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence about the social-media diet versus recommended changes, anchoring on his stated motivations (grandchildren, avoiding dialysis, avoiding another hospitalization)

Gently and non-judgmentally elicit a fuller alcohol history; once disclosed, explain in plain language how nightly/binge drinking can affect blood pressure, fluid balance, and interact with his heart and blood pressure medicines, and encourage him to share this with his cardiologist
Review the metoprolol refill record with him, normalize forgetting, and problem-solve concrete reminder strategies (e.g., pairing refill pickup with a routine household task, pharmacy auto-refill)
Involve his wife as a support resource for meal planning and reminders while coaching the couple on letting Gayle answer first before she fills in gaps
Arrange follow-up nutrition visit to reassess diet pattern, denture adaptation, and refer back to primary care/cardiology for the unexpectedly low HbA1c, low BP, and newly disclosed alcohol use
redFlags: BP 83/70 mmHg in a patient on four antihypertensive/cardiac medications plus newly disclosed heavier alcohol intake
Potassium 5.0 mmol/L in a patient with CKD and diabetic nephropathy
Unexplained discrepancy between HbA1c 3.4% and his diagnosed prediabetes/insulin regimen
Newly disclosed heavy episodic drinking (half a six-pack alone on at least three occasions this month) not yet communicated to his cardiologist
Two undisclosed metoprolol refill lapses this year in a patient with ischemic heart disease
educationPoints: 'Natural' or 'sugar-free' labels do not automatically make a food safe for his kidneys, blood sugar, or blood pressure; checking sodium and potassium on labels matters too
Canned soups and deli meats, while convenient and soft, are often high in sodium, which is important to watch with his kidney condition
Timing meals consistently with his insulin doses can help avoid skipped doses and swings in blood sugar
Soft doesn't have to mean processed: there are nutrient-rich, easy-to-chew options like soft-cooked vegetables, eggs, and blended foods that fit his denture and his health needs
Alcohol can affect blood pressure and interact with his heart and blood pressure medicines, so sharing his actual drinking pattern with his cardiology team is important for his safety
Skipping a pill is not 'balanced out' by eating well that day; medications and diet work together, not as substitutes for each other
Missing a refill isn't a moral failing — simple reminder systems (like pharmacy auto-refill or pairing pickups with routine errands) can help close that gap

mismatches.patientClaim: Gayle initially reports missing his metoprolol only on days he feels foggy or overwhelmed, attributing all missed doses to how he feels (h4, a4)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows the metoprolol succinate refill was late by about 2-3 weeks on two separate occasions this year, independent of symptom days
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported reasons for nonadherence may be incomplete; cross-checking refill records can reveal logistical gaps (forgetting to refill) that need a different solution (e.g., auto-refill) than symptom-related skipping alone

mismatches.patientClaim: Gayle initially states he drinks 'just a beer or two' on weekends (s6)
mismatches.recordEvidence: On gentle repeated questioning during the same visit, he discloses drinking most nights, sometimes 4-5 beers when stressed, and finishing half a six-pack alone on at least three occasions this month (s7, s8, s9)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Initial minimization of alcohol intake is common; nonjudgmental, repeated open-ended questioning can reveal a pattern with significant implications for blood pressure and medication interactions that the patient did not think to mention to his cardiologist
